Keep this sheet open during the labs. It covers the Week 5 concepts from Chapter 6, plus access analysis with buffers and travel-time areas, which the textbook skips (marked \*).

## Key terms

| Term | Means |
|---|---|
| Primary sector | Extracting raw materials: farming, fishing, mining, logging |
| First agricultural revolution | Domestication of plants and animals, from about 9000 BCE, in several hearths |
| Second agricultural revolution | Crop rotation, enclosure, machinery and purchased inputs, about 1750–1880 |
| Green revolution | High-yield seeds, fertilizers and irrigation from the mid-1900s; later GMOs |
| Columbian exchange | Movement of crops, animals, people and diseases between hemispheres after 1492 |
| Comparative advantage | Places specialize in what they produce most efficiently, using land, labour and capital, then trade |
| Commercial agriculture | Farming to sell for cash |
| Subsistence agriculture | Farming mainly to feed the household |
| Intensive / extensive | High yield per area / low yield over large areas |
| Von Thünen model | Land use forms rings around a market, set by revenue per area, land cost and transport cost |
| Hunger | A prolonged lack of food; shows as stunting and underweight |
| Food security | Reliable access to enough food of the quality and diversity needed for health |
| Food desert | Low income plus low access to healthy food (see definition below) |
| Food loss / food waste | Lost between farm and market / discarded by retailers or consumers |

**Textbook food desert definition (US):** census tracts where at least 100 households are low income, have no vehicle, and are more than half a mile from a supermarket.

## Von Thünen rings, from the market outward

1. Market gardening and dairy: perishable, high revenue per area
2. Forest: heavy fuelwood and timber
3. Grain crops: lower revenue, easy to transport
4. Livestock grazing: needs the most land

## Watch for these traps

- **Supply is not access.** World food supply per person has risen, yet hunger persists where people are poor or markets are disrupted.
- **Access is not diet.** Opening a supermarket does not always change what people eat; cost and habits matter too.
- **Buffers overstate access.** Straight lines ignore roads, terrain and transport.
- **Store lists vary.** Check which stores a dataset counts as healthy food sources.

## Measuring access\*

| Method | Includes | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Buffer | Everything within a straight-line distance | Quick screening, or where travel is truly direct |
| Travel-time area | Everything reachable along roads within a set time, walking or driving | Realistic access, especially in rural areas |
| Nearest facility | Distance or time from each home to its closest facility | Ranking who is farthest from services |

**Workflow:** draw areas around facilities → overlay population or households → count who falls outside → map the gap as a rate.

## ArcGIS Online quick steps

Sign in at [emory.maps.arcgis.com](https://emory.maps.arcgis.com). Login instructions and free Esri training are on the [Emory GIS resources page](https://gis.ecds.emory.edu/). Esri renames menus from time to time, so if a label differs, look for the nearest match.

| To do this | Go to |
|---|---|
| Draw straight-line buffers | Analysis → Tools → Create Buffers. Choose the store layer, distance and units; dissolve overlapping buffers if you want one area (uses credits) |
| Draw travel-time areas | Analysis → Tools → Create Drive-Time Areas. Choose walking or driving time and the time breaks (uses credits) |
| Count people inside or outside | Analysis → Tools → Summarize Within, with tracts or population points as the summarized layer (uses credits) |
| Select tracts that meet a definition | Select the tract layer → Filter → add conditions, for example low-income households ≥ 100 and households without a vehicle ≥ 100 |
| Find each home's nearest store | Analysis → Tools → Find Nearest (uses credits) |

Analysis tools spend credits. Test on a small area first.

## Public health case: Wong et al. 2021 (Vukuzazi)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| People aged 15+ screened, May 2018 – Nov 2019 | 17,118 |
| At least one active disease | 52.1% |
| HIV | 34.2% |
| Elevated blood pressure | 23.0% |
| Elevated blood glucose | 8.5% |
| Active tuberculosis / lifetime tuberculosis | 1.4% / 21.8% |
| Appropriate treatment and optimal control | HIV 78.1%; blood pressure 42.5%; active TB 29.6%; blood glucose 7.1% |

Main finding: infectious and non-communicable disease epidemics converge in one rural population. HIV is well treated; the other conditions are poorly diagnosed and controlled. Patterns differed by sex, age and place.

## Critical lens

- Plantation agriculture in the Americas relied on enslaved and indentured labour. Many former colonies still depend on one export crop.
- South Africa's 1913 Natives Land Act restricted Black land ownership to about 7% of the country, later about 13%, leaving crowded rural reserves with little farmland.
- Some advocates prefer **"food apartheid"** to "food desert", to name the policies behind unequal access.

## Six questions to ask any food access map

1. Supply, access or quality?
2. Straight-line buffer or travel time?
3. Walking, driving or public transit?
4. Which stores count as "healthy food"?
5. Who lacks a vehicle, and where?
6. What history made access unequal?

## Textbook corrections

- The chapter credits Old World to New World diffusion for Ireland's potato. The potato is a New World crop that spread *from* the Americas.
- It calls the peppers in Indian curries "Old World peppers". Chili peppers are New World crops.
